patient.chief_complaint: Acute onset diplopia, ataxia, and inability to walk in a 28-year-old, with no limb weakness but complete areflexia.
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. D. is a 28-year-old previously healthy man presenting to the emergency department with a 4-day history of progressive neurological symptoms. Three weeks prior, he had a mild upper respiratory illness lasting 5 days. Four days ago, he noticed horizontal double vision that worsened rapidly. By day 2, he developed drooping of both eyelids. On day 3, he noticed severe balance problems — he fell twice and has been holding walls to walk. He denies any limb weakness: his arms and legs feel strong. He denies any headache, vomiting, or confusion. He has no back pain. He denies any recent travel or tick exposure. Emergency providers initially suspected a posterior fossa stroke given the ophthalmoplegia and ataxia. Brain CT was unremarkable. On examination, the striking finding is the triad of complete ophthalmoplegia, severe ataxia, and complete areflexia in an otherwise healthy 28-year-old with normal limb strength.

specialized_test.impression: NCS consistent with Miller Fisher syndrome variant of GBS: isolated sensory SNAP reduction/absence, absent H-reflex and F-waves indicating proximal involvement, but relatively preserved motor CMAPs and conduction velocities. This pattern is classic for MFS where the target is GQ1b-bearing cranial nerves (III, IV, VI) and dorsal root ganglia rather than motor fibers.

output.summary: Miller Fisher syndrome is a GBS variant caused by anti-GQ1b antibodies targeting ocular motor cranial nerves. Typically self-limiting with good prognosis. IVIG or plasmapheresis accelerates recovery. Monitor for overlap with classic GBS (20%) and Bickerstaff encephalitis.

key_reasoning_points: The diagnostic puzzle: ophthalmoplegia + ataxia + areflexia WITHOUT limb weakness in a young patient initially suggests posterior fossa stroke — but MRI is normal
Anti-GQ1b IgG >95% sensitive and specific for Miller Fisher syndrome — the key diagnostic test
GQ1b is expressed at high levels in oculomotor nerve paranodal myelin — explains why cranial nerves are selectively affected
NCS shows preserved motor CMAPs because limb motor nerves are not the primary target — sensory and cranial nerve pathology predominates
Overlap with classic GBS occurs in 20% — monitor for developing limb weakness and respiratory compromise
